source_artifacts.locator: approval queue (as shown to the analyst)

capabilities.target: user principal's MFA methods and temporary access pass
chat channel of the person who opened the ticket

inputs.source: Support ticket submitted via email, including by contractors and vendors

instructions.note: The procedure tells the agent to reset MFA and send the temp pass to 'the person who opened the ticket' without ever requiring that this person be verified as the account owner, baking impersonation risk into the stated goal.

controls.name: Service desk analyst approval gate for idp.reset_mfa
controls.decay_rationale: The analyst sees the raw target, requester, and full ticket text (approval_review_mode: raw_action), so a stronger model cannot change what is displayed. However, effectiveness is not truly model-capability-independent in practice: all three displayed fields originate from the same untrusted ticket/email, with no independent identity channel, and approval volume (~200 requests/analyst/shift) creates approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403). It only gates cap.mfa_reset, not the subsequent cap.send_temp_pass egress.

controls.name: Bind temp-pass delivery to the account owner's registered contact, not the ticket requester
controls.decay_rationale: If the destination is pulled from the account's registered contact record in the system of record rather than from agent- or ticket-supplied data, it does not depend on model behavior and does not decay.

controls.name: Out-of-band identity verification before a reset is eligible for approval
controls.decay_rationale: Adds a channel independent of the ticket text itself, but is only as strong as the out-of-band channel used; if that channel is also easily spoofed (e.g., a reply-to email) a capable or well-resourced attacker could still route around it.

findings.title: Confused-deputy MFA reset: untrusted ticket drives credential reset and sends the temp pass to the ticket submitter, not the verified account owner (TC4-adjacent)

attack_path.note: Untrusted ticket submitted by email; the requester field is just the email sender, so it can be a contractor, vendor, or a spoofed/impersonated identity.
Agent looks up the named user to populate the reset request.
Analyst approval is required here, but the analyst reviews only the same ticket-supplied requester, target, and body, with no independent identity check.
Unapproved, automatic egress: the temp pass is sent to whoever opened the ticket, not to the verified account owner, once the reset is approved.

findings.residual_rationale: Crediting ctl.analyst_approval alone (raw_action gate on cap.mfa_reset) would put the floor at moderate (critical minus two tiers). We hold residual at high instead because that gate covers only the credential_access step and is based entirely on ticket-supplied data (requester, body) that is itself the untrusted artifact under attack, with no independent identity channel; and because cap.send_temp_pass, the actual egress of the credential to an unverified recipient, has no approval gate at all and fires automatically once the reset is approved. Combined with approval volume of roughly 200 requests per analyst per shift, this matches the documented pattern behind real helpdesk MFA-reset social-engineering breaches.

forecast.watch_signal: The approval requirement on idp.reset_mfa is removed, made optional, or auto-approved for 'trusted' or high-volume senders to manage queue backlog; or autonomy for this capability is raised beyond A2 so resets no longer require analyst sign-off.

evidence.observation: Instructions direct the agent to look up the user, reset MFA, and send the temp pass to whoever opened the ticket, with no requirement to verify the ticket opener is the account owner.
Contractors and vendors can email tickets in, and the requester field is just the email sender, so the identity shown to the analyst is attacker-controllable.

The temporary pass goes to whoever opened the ticket, not the account owner, and this delivery step (chat.send_temp_pass) has no approval gate of its own; it runs automatically once the reset is approved.
Two analysts approve roughly 400 requests per shift (about 200 each), a volume consistent with the approval-fatigue pattern documented in real helpdesk social-engineering MFA-reset incidents.

The queue shows target, requester, and ticket text as raw_action review, but all three fields originate from the same untrusted ticket/email under attacker control, with no independent identity-verification channel shown.

recommendations.action: Bind the temporary pass destination to the account owner's pre-registered contact record, not the ticket requester/email-sender field; refuse to auto-send and flag the mismatch to the analyst if they differ.

Require an out-of-band identity verification step (e.g., callback to a number already on file, or manager/HR attestation) before a reset request becomes eligible for analyst approval, so approval is not based solely on self-reported ticket content.

Add a dedicated approval gate on chat.send_temp_pass (or fold recipient verification into the existing gate) so delivery of the credential is independently reviewed rather than automatic once the reset is approved.
Track per-analyst approval volume and automatically flag MFA-reset requests originating from external or contractor-submitted tickets for mandatory secondary review to counter approval fatigue.

rating.rationale: The ticket intake is untrusted (contractors and vendors can email tickets in, and the requester field is just the email sender), and the path reaches an S3 sink by two independent measures: cap.mfa_reset is a credential_access action, and cap.send_temp_pass is egress of confidential credential material. Inherent risk is critical. The only control is analyst approval on the reset step; because it is raw_action review it avoids the automatic moderate floor, but it reviews data that is itself the untrusted ticket content with no independent identity channel, and it does not cover the subsequent unguarded delivery of the pass to the ticket opener. Residual is therefore held at high rather than the moderate the control credit alone would imply. If that one control is removed, bypassed, or loosened as queue volume grows, the design reverts to its critical inherent risk, which is why ctl.analyst_approval is the single control to monitor and strengthen first.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts (system prompt, approval-queue mockup, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No tool manifest or MCP/runtime configuration was provided; capability scope and whether chat.send_temp_pass is actually unguarded are inferred from prose and the runtime notes rather than verified configuration, which limits confidence to medium.
No information was provided on whether analysts have any identity-verification channel beyond the ticket text and requester field; the assessment assumes they do not.
